title: Oscar and the Vow
premise: Cellist Elodie Winterbourne, humiliated by a career-ending performance and a broken engagement in the same week, retreats to her grandmother's crumbling bakery in the coastal town of Gullwick, where the lease expires in ninety days. To survive the Winterbourne family reunion—and her mother's campaign to marry her off to a suitable heir—she recruits Oscar Hale, the gruff baker next door who needs her cello-playing to save his failing business, into a fake courtship. As their staged romance deepens into something real, Elodie discovers her grandmother's will ties the bakery's inheritance to whoever keeps it alive, forcing a choice between reclaiming her music on her own terms or losing Oscar to his own vow of never needing anyone. At the reunion's final dinner, Elodie publicly ends the pretense, plays the piece that once destroyed her, and proposes a real partnership: they marry neither duty nor convenience, but each other, saving both bakery and heart.
about_author: Juniper Dravenmoor is the pen name of a former orchestral librarian who traded concert halls for coastal kitchens and writes love stories where duty is the villain and dessert is the alibi. She lives in a drafty house full of sheet music and sourdough starter.

chapters.title: The Broken String
chapters.summary: Elodie's POV. Mid-concert at London's Meridian Hall, Elodie's hands seize; she walks offstage mid-sonata as her fiancé's text of condolence-cum-breakup glows backstage. Devastated, she flees to Gullwick, inheriting temporary custody of her late grandmother's bakery and its expiring lease. Emotional beat: collapse and flight—the heart as a muscle she vows to train into obedience.

chapters.title: Flour and Ash
chapters.summary: Oscar's POV. Oscar Hale, the baker whose shop adjoins the Winterbourne bakery, resents the city heiress who let the ovens go cold for three years. But when he catches Elodie playing cello alone at midnight—music drifting over flour-dusted counters—he hears what grief sounds like. He offers a gruff truce: bread lessons for honesty. Beat: reluctant curiosity softening contempt.

chapters.title: Terms of Engagement
chapters.summary: Elodie's POV. The reunion invitation arrives: three days, one estate, her mother armed with eligible bachelors. Elodie impulsively tells her mother she's seeing someone—then begs Oscar to play the part. He agrees only if she performs Fridays at his café to draw customers before his own lease dies. Beat: a bargain struck, both pretending it means nothing.

chapters.title: Rehearsal
chapters.summary: Oscar's POV. Fake-dating rehearsals: hand-holding practice over proofing dough, invented first-date stories, laughter that isn't in the script. Oscar reveals why he never lets anyone stay—his father's debts devoured their family bakery once, and he swore a vow of self-sufficiency. Beat: intimacy by accident; the first crack in the performance.

chapters.title: The Winterbourne Estate
chapters.summary: Elodie's POV. Day one of the reunion. Her mother parades hedge-fund heir Charles Pemberton; Elodie deploys Oscar like armor. But her aunt corners her with news: Grandmother's will names an heir conditional on keeping the bakery 'alive in spirit and in trade'—and the family intends to contest it. Beat: belonging offered on hostile terms.

chapters.title: Dessert
chapters.summary: Oscar's POV. The fake date becomes too real by dessert: dancing under string lights, an almost-kiss interrupted by Charles's pointed toast mocking 'the help.' Oscar nearly blows the cover defending her; Elodie covers with a kiss that neither of them pretends afterward was acting. Beat: the lie turns true and terrifies them both.

chapters.title: Ninety Days
chapters.summary: Elodie's POV. Back home, the lease deadline looms and the family's lawyers circle. Elodie finds her grandmother's letters revealing she once gave up a concert career for love—and regretted the silence, not the choice. Meanwhile Elodie realizes she's falling for Oscar but can't tell if he feels anything real. Beat: longing tangled with fear of repeating history.

chapters.title: The Vow
chapters.summary: Oscar's POV. Oscar learns the family will drop the contest if Elodie returns to London and signs the bakery over to them—a life he can't offer her. Honoring his vow of never needing anyone, he pushes her away, claiming the romance was business. Elodie, gutted, prepares to leave. Beat: the dark night—duty masquerading as protection.

chapters.title: The Final Performance
chapters.summary: Elodie's POV. At the reunion's closing dinner, Elodie refuses to sign. Instead she takes out her cello and plays the sonata that broke her—hands steady this time—declaring that she inherits nothing by their permission and everything by her grandmother's intent. Then she turns to Oscar, publicly ending the 'fake': she doesn't want borrowed pieces of him, she wants the whole heart. Beat: climax—courage reclaimed, truth spoken.

chapters.title: Rising
chapters.summary: Alternating POVs. Oscar breaks his vow, chasing her to the dock as her taxi idles: he'd rather need her than be safe without her. They renew the leases together—her inheritance secured, his café merged with her bakery, Friday concerts restored. Epilogue beat: a year later, bread rises beside cello cases; two hearts, fully spent, finally belonging.
